Τῶν κινουμένων τὰ μέν τινα ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχει τὴν τῆς κινήσεως αἰτίαν, ἕτερα δὲ ἔξωϑεν μόνον κινεῖται. ἔξωϑεν μὲν οὖν μόνον κινεῖται τὰ φορητά, οἷον ξύλα καὶ λίϑοι καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ὑπὸ ἕξεως μόνης συνεχομένη ὕλη. ὑπεξηῃηρήσϑω δὲ νῦν τοῦ λόγου τὸ κίνησιν λέγειν τὴν δύσιν τῶν σωμάτων, ἐπεὶ μὴ χρεία τούτου πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον. ἐν ξαυτοῖς δὲ ἔχει τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ζῷα καὶ φυτὰ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὅσα ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς συνέχεται: ἐξ ὧν φασιν εἶναι xci τὰ μέταλλα, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτοκίνητόν ἐστι, τάχα δὲ καὶ αἱ πηγαί. τῶν δὲ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ἐχοντῶν τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν" ἐξ ξαυτῶν μὲν τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα. καὶ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν xiνεῖται τὰ ἔμψυχα, φαντασίας ἐγγινομένης ὁρμὴν προκαλουμένης. xal πάλιν Ev τισι τῶν ζῴων φαντασίαι γίνονται ὁρμὴν προ καλούμεναι, φύσεως φανταστικῆς τεταγμένως κινούσης τὴν ὁρμήν, ος ἐν τῷ ἀράχνῃ φαντασία τοῦ ὑφαίνειν γίνεται καὶ ὁρμὴ ἀκολουϑεῖ ἐπὶ τὸ ὑφαίνειν, τῆς φανταστικῆς αὐτοῦ φύσεως τεταγμένως ἐπὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸν προκαλουμένης xal οὐδενὸς ἄλλου μετὰ τὴν φανταστικὴν αὖτοῦ φύσιν πεπιστευμένου τοῦ ζῴου, καὶ ἐν τῇ μελίσσῃ ἐπὶ τὸ χηροσπλαστεῖν. 3(2). pass_a_gloss: He will say in the ecclesiastical preaching that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to live well and to flee from sin in every way, so that we may understand, having been consoled by the Lord, that we take the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold the notion of it, so that, having been accurately clarified, the thing being sought may be presented. For of the things being moved, some have in themselves the cause of the movement, but others are moved only from outside. Therefore, the things being carried are moved only from outside, such as wood and stones and all matter being held together by habit only. But let the word about the movement of bodies be left out now, since it is not necessary for the present subject. And animals and plants and all things being held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves: from which they say metals are, and besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from outside themselves: from outside themselves, indeed, the non-living things, but from themselves, the living things. And the living things are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring, an impulse being provoked. And again, in some of the animals, fantasies occur, an impulse being provoked, the natural fantasy moving the impulse, as in the spider, a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the fantasy of its nature moving it to this very thing, and no other thing being believed by the animal after its fantasy, and in the bee, to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason with respect to the fantasy of nature, approving the fantasies and rejecting some, but accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are starting-points to contemplate the good and the bad, following which, having contemplated the good and the bad, we choose the good, but turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy, having given ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy, according to the opposite. But it must not be unknown that the greater part of the nature being ordered to all things is in the animals, and for the most part, or for the lesser part, so that it is near, as I might say, the work of the rational in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing being subjected to this or that from outside, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is, to be sure, not in our power: but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise, is not the work of another, but of the reason in us, either working in us according to the starting-points to the impulses being provoked to the good and to duty, or turning us away to the opposite.
pass_b_english: He will declare that the ecclesiastical proclamation contains the word concerning God's righteous anointing, and that this word—once it is believed to be true—also summons us to live well and to flee sin in every way. Its purpose is that, consoled by the Lord, we may take hold of what is the most necessary problem. To grasp what "self-moved" means, we must first unfold the concept itself; only when it has been accurately clarified will the matter under investigation be properly presented. Among things that move, some possess the cause of their motion within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried—wood, stones, and all matter held together merely by habit—are moved solely from outside. We may set aside the discussion of bodily locomotion for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals, plants, and everything held together by nature or soul have the cause of their motion within themselves. Some say metals belong here as well, and add that fire is self-moved, perhaps also springs. Among those having the cause of motion in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves. The non-living are moved from outside themselves; the living are moved from themselves. Living things move from themselves when a fantasy arises that provokes an impulse. Again, in certain animals fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with their imaginative nature moving the impulse in an ordered way. In the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs, and an impulse follows to weave, its imaginative nature urging it to this very act, and the creature believes in nothing else beyond its own imaginative nature. In the bee the fantasy drives it to shape wax. The rational animal, however, possesses reason alongside its imaginative nature. Reason judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Because the nature of reason contains starting-points for contemplating the good and the bad, we—following those starting-points—contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad. When we give ourselves to practicing the good we are praiseworthy; when we do the opposite we are blameworthy. Yet we must not overlook that the larger part of the nature ordered toward all things is found in animals, whether to a greater or lesser degree. It is therefore near, so to speak, to the work of the rational in tracking dogs and war horses. To be subjected to this or that external thing, which stirs a fantasy in us one way or another, is admittedly not in our power. But to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise is not the work of anyone else; it belongs to the reason within us—either working in us according to those starting-points toward impulses provoked to the good and to duty, or turning us away toward the opposite.
